text: Teaching letter sounds step by step is one of the most tested ideas in education. Decades of studies agree that systematic phonics helps children learn to read, and Choo Choo Training is built on it.
Frequent, short practice beats occasional long sessions. Find a regular time each day for a lesson.
Speaking is the foundation of reading. When your child answers with one word ("milk," "play"), ask for a whole sentence, and model it: "I want milk." "I want to play."
Children learn best by seeing or hearing it done first. If your child is stuck on a sound, say it first, then invite them: "You try!"
Strong readers look at every letter in a word. When your child gets stuck, say "Let's sound it out."
Children blend better when sounds are stretched together ("mmmaaat") than chopped apart ("m... a... t"). Chopping makes them forget the first sound by the time they reach the last.
Say /m/ as "mmm," not "muh." Extra "uh" sounds make blending harder: "buh-a-tuh" doesn't sound like "bat." Keep stop sounds short and crisp, like a tiny hiccup.
Sound games work noticeably better when letters are involved. Say "sun," then have your child find the letter that makes the first sound.
Spelling practice makes children better readers, not just better spellers. Say "map" and have your child build it with magnet letters.
Mixing up b and d is a normal stage of learning to read, common through about age 7. On its own, it isn't a sign of dyslexia. If it continues into third grade, mention it to the teacher.
Letter names can mislead. "W" is called "double-u," so some children think it says /d/. When reading, use letter sounds ("this says /w/") instead of names.
Short e (bed) and short i (big) sound so alike that many children mix them up. Play "pin or pen?" and "bit or bet?" Listening for the difference helps reading too.
Children often read the first letter and guess the rest. Try the "change one letter" game: sat, sit, sip, tip, tap. It trains them to look at every letter.
Short, spaced practice beats long sessions. Ten to fifteen minutes a day works better than an hour on the weekend.
Rereading the same short story builds fluency. Read a page aloud first, then let your child read it 3 or 4 times over a few days.
Most "sight words" are only partly tricky. In "said," only the "ai" is unusual. Sound out the regular letters together, and learn just the tricky part by heart.
How you correct matters. Point to the exact letter, say its sound, and have your child reread the word. That works better than a general "try again."
Reading is two skills: sounding out words and understanding language. Reading aloud to your child builds the second. Read books above their level and chat about new words.
A typical child reads about 60 words a minute at the end of first grade and 100 by the end of second. These are averages, not deadlines; steady progress is what matters.
A fun way to speed up your child's learning is to find letters "out in the wild" during your day. Show them a cereal box or their favorite book and ask if they can find "mmm."
